source.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
source.authors: K. Cobbe; V. Kosaraju; Mo Bavarian; Mark Chen; Heewoo Jun; Lukasz Kaiser; Matthias Plappert; Jerry Tworek; Jacob Hilton; Reiichiro Nakano; Christopher Hesse; John D. Schulman

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream math-task performance across GPT-3 model sizes, using solve rate rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. on scaling trends, but those cited results are not this study's findings. It reports its own downstream solve-rate sweep by model size in Figure 2; values are plotted without readable numeric data in the supplied text. It also reports a qualitative model-size comparison and an extrapolation based on an assumed log-linear trend.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-size sweep (GPT-3 3B, 6B, 12B, 175B) and training-set-size sweep, finetuning each on GSM8K and measuring test solve rate. That bears on V6 (downstream performance improving with scale) in a new setting: finetuned multi-step math. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The size range is only about 1.8 orders of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that verification significantly improves GSM8K performance over finetuning, about equal to a 30x model-size increase, and scales better with data. Token-level verifiers overfit less, and dropout helps all methods. The 175B-over-smaller-models result and the 10^16-parameter figure are side observations; the latter is explicitly a naive log-linear extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream GSM8K solve rate after finetuning across model sizes, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and training-set size are varied; Figure 2 reports mean and standard deviation across 3 runs.

fits_no_version.finding: 6B verification slightly outperforms finetuned 175B, a boost equivalent to about a 30x increase in model size. Verifiers also scale better with data than finetuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time verification and search change the effective scaling curve of downstream task performance.

record.problems: The relevant model-size results are plotted without numeric values in the supplied text. The extrapolated 80% estimate assumes a log-linear trend and is not validated by a larger run. The measured outcome is downstream solve rate, not pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss. No fitted power law is reported, and the authors only assume a log-linear trend in parameters. The size range is under two orders of magnitude.
All parts; no pretraining loss is measured.
All parts; the extrapolation is never checked against a larger run.
All parts; finetuning-data scaling is measured as solve rate, not loss.

missing.what: Statement that solve rate vs training-set size does not follow a log-linear trend, and that 175B likely needs at least 2 more orders of magnitude of data to reach 80%.
Qualitative note that larger models make fewer arithmetic mistakes than smaller models.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1–r20 are figure-only values from Figure 2 and cannot be read numerically from the text. They remain cannot_determine, so they were removed from the supports label. The original limits_scope label on r22 was dropped because the extrapolation is an assumption, not a result showing a limitation. Evidence for V6 is weak: four model sizes, a qualitative statement, and no fitted law.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream solve rate across model sizes on GSM8K, not predictability from pretraining loss or a fitted power law across orders of magnitude.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: model with 10^16 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Naively extrapolated the model-size trend assuming a log-linear relationship.
rows.value: estimated to be required to reach an 80% solve rate
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: This is an explicitly conditional extrapolation, not an observed run.
rows.check: This is the authors' own projection under an assumed log-linear trend (10^16 params for 80%), not a measured result. It should not ground a verdict and is not evidence of a limitation.

relationships.condition: GPT-3 models 3B–175B finetuned on the full GSM8K training set, model-size axis
relationships.reason: Solve rate rises with model size, and 175B 'significantly outperforms the smaller models' (r21). The authors treat the trend as roughly log-linear in parameters.
relationships.display_finding: Solve rates increased roughly linearly with log parameters, and the 175B model significantly outperformed smaller models.

relationships.reason: The text says performance 'does not appear to follow a log-linear trend' in training-set size, so extrapolating along data is hard. No row records this; the verdict is based on the Section 4.1 text.
relationships.display_finding: Performance does not appear log-linear in training-set size, making extrapolation along the data dimension difficult.
